author_bibtex: Guan, Shaopeng and Cao, Youliang and Zhang, Yuan
approach: Paillier additive encryption, searchable encryption, Bloom indexes, and Fabric access policies
contribution: Ciphertext processing and controlled record retrieval
boundary: Retrieved records are decrypted before authorized sharing. Search leakage, recipient misuse, and computation correctness are not established.
control: Encrypted records, search index, membership and key release
trust: Record service, key holders, and authorized recipients

author_bibtex: Gupta, Mansi and Kumar, Mohit and Gupta, Yash
approach: DenseNet local training, hierarchical model aggregation, signed updates, and IPFS references
contribution: Hospital model sharing with blockchain coordination
evaluation: Two-client, 15-round learning experiment and image-classification comparisons
boundary: Hashing and signatures do not provide encryption. Classification accuracy does not establish update confidentiality or resistance to model poisoning.
actor: Hospitals, federated routers, backend aggregators, validators
control: Training data, model updates, and signed storage references

author_bibtex: Ghosh, Abir and Mukhopadhyay, Indraneel and Chakraborty, Subhalaxmi
approach: Bank gateway checks consent, records exchanges, and compares authorized and reported fields through regulatory supervision
contribution: Consent agreement, exchange audit, and withdrawal workflow
evaluation: Bank emulation with 4--10 nodes and 10--50 customer-count parameters
boundary: Supervision covers recorded gateway exchanges. It does not establish complete capture of other transfers or deletion by recipients.
control: Consent agreement and reported shared fields

author_bibtex: Qu, Xiao and Yang, Zhexuan and Chen, Zeng and Sun, Guozi
approach: Patient decrypts an IPFS record, re-encrypts it for sharing, and releases a temporary key. Traceable ring signatures record stages
evaluation: Transaction-load, user-count, record-size, and ring-signature experiments
boundary: Patient mediation does not prevent recipient copying or establish downstream deletion. Signature results cover their stated relation.
control: Record ciphertext, temporary key, and signed sharing stages
trust: Patient key custody, institutions, and registration authority

author_bibtex: Rao, Krishna Prasad N and Selvan, C.
approach: Attribute-authority keys, encrypted IPFS records, recipient tokens, and contract consent checks
evaluation: Synthetic datasets of 10--1,000 records with encryption, key-generation, and storage measurements
boundary: Withdrawal has no specified key/ciphertext update that invalidates previously released data. Cryptographic timings do not establish legal compliance.
control: Consent state, attribute keys, and genomic ciphertext

author_bibtex: Scaramuzza, Filippo and Tonnarelli, Marco and Tamburri, Damian A. and van den Heuvel, Willem-Jan
approach: Contract permission states and a zk-SNARK proving knowledge of a Pedersen-committed secret
contribution: Permission approvals, revocation, and commitment verification
evaluation: Functional requirements and single-machine cryptographic benchmarks
boundary: The paper identifies RSA-512, trusted setup, public participant links, and trusted off-chain erasure as limits. The proof does not establish factual data use.
actor: Data subject, controller, requesting party, prover/verifier
control: Permission status, encrypted metadata, and commitment witness
trust: Setup-secret destruction, metadata encryption, and off-chain erasure

author_bibtex: Ferreira, Joao C. and Correia, Ricardo and Rosário, Luís and Vila, Alberto
approach: DID/VC identity, issuer allowlists, purpose/time consent checks, bundle hashes, and provenance logs
contribution: Gateway consent enforcement and record-linked audit handles
blockchain_platform: Fabric or EVM L2 alternatives, deployment not consistently identified
evaluation: Reported 300-request comparison. Table 3 labels the results illustrative
boundary: Dataset/domain descriptions are inconsistent. Hashes do not prove LLM-summary correctness or complete inputs. Gateway, issuer, and cache behavior remain conditions.
actor: Patient, credential issuer, FHIR service, MCP gateway, requester
control: Credential status, purpose/scope/time consent, and returned bundle
trust: Issuer allowlists, gateway enforcement, and revocation caches

author_bibtex: Ayala-Tipan, Carlos and Suntaxi, Gabriela and Caiza-Jimenez, Boris and Guzman-Castillo, Adan F. and Flores, Denys A.
approach: Global and company-specific hash-linked records with consent states and described key release
contribution: Consent creation, editing, and withdrawal interface
evaluation: Eight synthetic block-count scenarios with 10 runs per scenario. Code available
boundary: Distributed consensus is not established. Withdrawal appends state and does not erase earlier blocks or recall released keys.
actor: Data subject, requesting company, application service
control: Consent state, recipient references, and described decryption keys

author_bibtex: Deepthika, K. and Shobana, G. and Reddy, Kumbam Venkat and {Srimathi S} and Kumar, Binod and Upadhyay, Shrikant
approach: Fabric authentication/permission checks and LSTM prediction of changing preferences
contribution: Proposed adaptive access decisions for health records
evaluation: CICIDS-2017/NSL-KDD experiments and reported consent-accuracy comparison
boundary: Consent labels and ground truth are not established from the intrusion datasets. Predicted preference is not explicit informed consent. Hashing is not confidentiality.
evidence_location: II.A--C, transaction algorithm; III, Table II
trust: Permission rules, preference labels, and requester authentication

author_bibtex: Gupta, Neha and Negi, Shweta and Rawat, Khyaty and Rawat, Megha
approach: Authorized issuers, contract issuance/checking/revocation, hashes, and digital signatures
evaluation: Stakeholder interviews/surveys and descriptive certificate-forgery comparison
boundary: The examined text does not establish a reproducible attack experiment or deployed topology. Selective disclosure and recipient confidentiality are not established.
evidence_location: III.A--B; IV.A--C, Figure 2 and Table V

author_bibtex: Hemlata, Kumari and Saxena, Sanjana and Barodiya, Divyansh and {Raman} and Pal, Sujata and Pal, Shantanu
approach: Hospital/patient Fabric approvals, event relay, RBAC, encrypted MinIO records, and RSA-wrapped AES keys
contribution: Dual approval before record-key release and propagated revocation
boundary: Removing a wrapped key from middleware does not invalidate a key already recovered by a recipient. The relay and key service remain enforcement dependencies.
evidence_location: III.A--C; IV, Algorithms 1--2; V, Tables II--III
actor: Hospital, patient, researcher, relay, key middleware
control: Dual consent states, record ciphertext, and released AES key
trust: Relay state propagation, middleware key custody, and recipients

author_bibtex: Lu, Xiuhua and Liu, Jing and Li, Fengyin and Zou, Jiazheng and Hou, Yuhao
approach: Linkable-claimable ring signatures and tripartite permission for chameleon-hash editing
contribution: Controlled score correction and optional reporter attribution
evaluation: Conditional security arguments and primitive benchmarks over 100 runs
boundary: Partial trust in review roles remains. Editing controls do not establish score truth, erasure of external copies, or consent to secondary processing.
control: Score transactions, reporter identity, and editing trapdoors
trust: Partially trusted review roles and stated cryptographic assumptions

author_bibtex: Liu, Yizhong and Zhao, Boyu and Zhao, Zedan and Liu, Jianwei and Lin, Xun and Wu, Qianhong and Susilo, W.
approach: Sharded DID/credential events, aggregate BFT certificates, and Merkle cross-field proofs
contribution: Decentralized identity verification across shard fields
evaluation: 30--60 nodes per shard with PBFT/HotStuff comparators. Best reported throughput 90,000 requests/s in simulation
boundary: Results concern message unforgeability/liveness under committee assumptions. Recorded credential-use identifiers permit linkage. Deactivation does not erase history.
actor: Holder, issuer, verifier, shard and leader committees
control: DID states, credential hashes, and cross-field certificates
trust: Authenticated channels, partial synchrony, and less than one-third Byzantine committee members

approach: DID/VC/presentation signatures, administrator-assigned role permissions, and IPFS records
contribution: Credential authentication and role-based medical-record access
evaluation: 50 repetitions and 10 parallel sessions for DID/credential gas and timing benchmarks
boundary: PII hashing and a signed presentation do not establish confidential attributes or cryptographic selective disclosure. Issuer/administrator trust and regulatory validation remain.
actor: Hospital/doctor issuer, patient holder, pharmacy/insurer verifier, role administrator
control: DID documents, signed credentials, and role permissions
trust: Issuer assertions, role administrator, Veramo keys, and IPFS availability
